title: Methods of Cooking Food
summary: Cooking makes food easy to digest; improves appearance, texture, colour, flavour and taste (acceptability); adds variety to meals; helps keep food longer (boiled milk, chapatti versus dough); and makes food safe by killing harmful micro-organisms. Pasteurisation heats milk to a high temperature and cools it quickly to destroy micro-organisms. Animal foods (meat, fish, eggs) must be cooked thoroughly, and cooked food should not be left over two hours at room temperature in summer.

Moist heat: boiling, simmering/stewing, steaming, pressure cooking. Dry heat: baking, roasting, grilling (200–300 degrees C, crisp texture and brown colour). Frying in oil or ghee: deep frying and shallow frying. Other methods: microwave and solar cooking.

Boiling cooks food in enough water; wash first, boil the water first, cover the food and use a lid, do not overcook, boil potatoes with skin; use the water for soup or gravy. Advantage: safe, simple, suits large-scale cooking; disadvantage: water-soluble nutrients are lost if the water is thrown. Stewing (simmering) cooks in a small quantity of water below boiling point for a long time; juices and nutrients are retained but it takes longer. Steaming cooks with the heat of water vapour (steamer, idli maker; idli, dhokla, momos); it is quick, conserves nutrients, colour and flavour and gives light food good for the sick, elderly and children. Pressure cooking uses steam under pressure above 100 degrees C; food cooks in about one-third the time, all bacteria are killed, fuel is saved and little water is needed; keep the weight vent and gasket clean.

Baking cooks in a heated closed oven (bread, cakes, biscuits); roasting is cooking directly on a hot tava, sand or fire (brinjal, maize, groundnuts, papad); grilling uses an iron grid over a glowing fire or between heated bars, slower than roasting (kababs, bati). Shallow frying uses a little oil (paratha, tikki); deep frying immerses the food in hot oil (pakora, puri, samosa). Fried food keeps longer but is difficult to digest and high in calories. Precautions: even pieces, heat oil well then lower heat, a few pieces at a time, drain on absorbent paper, strain and store used oil, avoid repeated heating. Microwave cooking is quick but needs electricity and may dry food. Solar cooking has no smoke or running cost and is eco-friendly but needs sunshine.

Vitamin A is oxidised in an open pan and destroyed by very hot oil (about 300 degrees C); cook in a covered pan. Vitamin B complex dissolves in washing and cooking water and is lost with cooking soda; riboflavin in milk is destroyed by sunlight. Vitamin C is destroyed by heat and oxidation, long exposure after cutting, washing after cutting, fine cutting, soda and discarded water. Proteins coagulate; overheating makes them dry, rubbery and hard to digest; acids toughen them (add at the end); protein and sugar cooked long (kheer) brown and lose quality. Oils and fats deteriorate when heated repeatedly. Minerals are lost when cooking water is thrown away.

Wash vegetables before cutting; scrape peels thin; cut into large pieces just before cooking; put into boiling water; use just enough water and do not throw it away; no cooking soda; tamarind or lemon juice helps conserve vitamins; cook rice in water that is fully absorbed; use a covered pan with a well-fitting lid; do not overcook; prefer the fastest method.

Enrichment or enhancement improves the nutrients of foods by simple, low-cost methods. Combination: eat foods of different groups together (rice with dal, khichri, missi roti, dhokla); pulses supply the amino acids cereals lack, so the protein becomes as good as milk protein. Fermentation: micro-organisms (curd, yeast or natural) change nutrients into simpler and better forms and create vitamin B complex and C; foods become soft and digestible (curd, idli, dhokla, bread, bhatura). Germination: soak grains 8–16 hours and sprout 12–24 hours in a moist cloth; digestibility and vitamins rise at no extra cost.

vsa: Write two differences between steaming and boiling methods of cooking.

In steaming the food does not touch water and is cooked by the heat of water vapour; in boiling the food is cooked in water. Steaming conserves nutrients, colour and flavour better, while in boiling water-soluble nutrients are lost if the water is thrown away.
April 2026

or: Give two advantages of including germinated foods in the meals.
Germination increases digestibility because some carbohydrates and proteins break into simpler forms, and it raises the nutritive value (vitamins) at no extra cost.

vsa: Write two differences between boiling and pressure cooking methods.

Boiling is done at 100 degrees C in an open pan with plenty of water and takes longer; pressure cooking is done above 100 degrees C in steam under pressure, takes about one-third of the time, saves fuel and needs little water. Pressure cooking kills all bacteria and loses less water-soluble vitamins.

Why is vitamin A lost when spinach is deep fried?
Vitamin A is fat-soluble and oxidised in contact with air; the temperature of deep frying (about 300 degrees C) destroys it rapidly. Cooking in a covered pan prevents its loss.
sa: Analyse any six reasons why nutrients of potatoes and methi are lost while cooking them.

Potatoes: peeling thickly removes minerals and vitamins just under the skin; cutting into small pieces; washing after cutting; boiling in a lot of water and discarding it (vitamin C, B and minerals); overcooking; frying at high temperature. Methi: cutting fine and washing after cutting; cooking in an open pan (vitamin A is oxidised and vitamin C is lost); deep frying (about 300 degrees C destroys vitamin A); using soda; long cooking.
Briefly explain any three methods of cooking food by dry heat.

Baking: food is cooked by hot air in a closed heated box, the oven (bread, cake, biscuits). Roasting: food is put directly on a hot tava, sand or fire and turned (brinjal, maize, groundnuts). Grilling: food is cooked on an iron grid over a glowing fire or between heated bars, more slowly than roasting (kababs, bati).
How are foods combined, fermented and germinated? State their advantages.

Combination: foods of different groups are eaten together or in one dish (khichri, missi roti); the protein quality improves without extra cost. Fermentation: micro-organisms from curd or yeast act on batter or dough (idli, dhokla); nutrients become simpler, vitamins B and C are formed and the food becomes soft and digestible. Germination: grains are soaked 8–16 hours and sprouted 12–24 hours in a moist cloth; digestibility and nutritive value increase at no extra cost.
Your mother is cooking chapatti, dal and vegetables for lunch. Give one suggestion each to enhance the nutritive value of each dish.

Chapatti: mix pulses or soya flour or add grated vegetables (missi roti, methi paratha) to improve proteins and vitamins. Dal: add spinach, moong or other vegetables, or combine with rice (khichri), and cook in a covered pan without soda. Vegetable: cut into large pieces just before cooking, cook in a covered pan with little water and use the water.
la: Give any five suggestions to conserve nutrients while preparing and cooking food.

(1) Wash vegetables before cutting, only as much as needed. (2) Scrape peels as thin as possible. (3) Cut into large pieces just before cooking. (4) Put vegetables into boiling water and use just enough water. (5) Use the extra water for soup or gravy. (6) Do not use cooking soda; a little lemon or tamarind helps keep vitamins. (7) Cook in a pan with a well-fitting lid and do not overcook.
Describe boiling, steaming and pressure cooking with one advantage of each.

Boiling: food is cooked in an adequate quantity of water; it is safe and simple. Steaming: food is cooked by the heat of water vapour in a steamer (idli, dhokla); it conserves nutrients, colour and flavour and the food is light and easily digested. Pressure cooking: food is cooked in steam under pressure above 100 degrees C; it needs only about one-third of the time, saves fuel and kills all bacteria.
